analysis.one_liner: Cuts the top corporate income tax rate to 20%.
analysis.headline: A bill to cut the top corporate tax rate to 20% was introduced by Sen. Mike Johanns in January 2011 and died in the Senate Finance Committee without a vote or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cut the top corporate income tax rate from 35% to 20%, with a 15% rate on the first $50,000 of corporate profits. It also would have cut the tax rate on personal service corporations — firms like law, accounting, and consulting practices. It never received a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and stayed there until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, large corporations and the shareholders who own their stock would have kept tens of billions of dollars a year that now goes to the Treasury. Personal service corporations — professional firms whose owners pay themselves out of the corporation — would also have paid a much lower rate on income flowing through.

how_it_helps.text: The bill cuts the maximum corporate tax rate to 20% of taxable income over $50,000, down from the 35% top rate in effect at the time.
The bill also applies the new rates to personal service corporations, not just regular corporations.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury — meaning taxpayers generally or future borrowers — would have received about $500 billion less in corporate tax revenue over a decade, according to standard estimates of corporate tax rate cuts. Over the long run, corporate taxes fall partly on shareholders (mostly wealthier households) and partly on workers through slightly lower wages, so the cost would be spread between the wealthy and everyone else through the budget.

drawbacks.text: Cutting the top corporate rate to 20% would sharply reduce federal revenue, worsening deficits or forcing offsetting tax increases or spending cuts elsewhere.

The flat 20% top rate is a large permanent tax cut concentrated on corporate profits, which accrue disproportionately to higher-income households; the bill included no offsetting revenue or reform to close tax loopholes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a large permanent tax cut to corporations without any mechanism to pay for it, so its costs land on the general budget while its benefits concentrate on corporate profits. Whatever gains flow to workers through lower corporate costs are indirect and much smaller than the direct gains to shareholders and professional service firms.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in January 2011, and it never received a hearing or a vote before the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Johanns (R-NE) introduced S. 85 on January 25, 2011.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance, where it stayed for the remainder of the Congress.
The bill had no cosponsors and no further legislative action was recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporate shareholders and professional service corporations are better off because the bill died, since the 35% corporate rate remained in effect rather than dropping to 20%. Federal revenue was preserved. The bill also carried a downside for ordinary people in its likely deficit effects, so its failure avoided that cost as well.

for.name: Sen. Mike Johanns (R-NE)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut the top corporate tax rate to 20%.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action; the bill was referred to the committee and never received a hearing or markup.

against.name: 111th Congress opposition (implied)
against.what_they_did: No senator cosponsored the bill, leaving it without visible support in either party.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors, so no party-line pattern emerged in any recorded vote or public support.

industries.note: The bill would have cut their tax rate on income above $50,000 from 35% to 20%, a permanent revenue reduction for the federal budget without offsets. Benefits concentrate on shareholders, who are disproportionately wealthier households.

industries.industry: Personal service corporations (law, accounting, consulting firms)
industries.note: The bill explicitly extended the 20% top rate to personal service corporations, giving professional firms a large tax cut on income flowing through.
Small incorporated businesses earning under $50,000 would pay 15%, a modest cut, though the bill's flat top rate mainly benefits larger, more profitable corporations.
